zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical identifications were checked after independent scan reading against Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html. The scan-derived transcription and English notes are this review's work.

lines.note: Wabibito is a sorrowful or impoverished person; the Portuguese explicitly combines sadness, poverty, and misery.

runs.text: Rogo, ou petição que ſe faz a al-

lines.note: Wabikoto is a plea or petition made to someone; the divided al- continues as alguem on the following row.
Completes alguem and specifies that the petition is made with self-humbling. This is an indented continuation of wabikoto, not a separate entry.

runs.text: Voz do que roga, ou intercede hu-

lines.note: Wabigoe names the voice of a person pleading or interceding; hu- begins the adverb humildemente across the physical line break.
Completes humildemente, then adds lamenting or becoming sad. The printed mezquinha is one word, rather than the OCR split mez quinha.
Wabishii describes being poor and miserable. The Portuguese continues the range of states on the next row.
Adds sadness and solitude to wabishii. These coordinated alternatives belong to the same adjective, not separate headwords.
Gives the derived nominal form wabishisa and the contracted adverbial wabishuu. The final apparent OCR i is punctuation rather than an additional Japanese syllable.

runs.text: Inclinado a chanyu de poucos pe-

lines.note: Wabizuki describes a taste for austere tea practice. The Portuguese chanyu occurs within the gloss, and poucos qualifies the small number of implements continued below.
Completes petrechos and continues with cobitos and poor walls, explaining the material simplicity of the tea setting. The unusual cobitos is retained as printed rather than modernized.
Waka is glossed as Japanese verses or songs. The Portuguese Iapão remains the historical country-name spelling.
Wakaba means new leaves of trees or herbs; folhas nouas directly matches the Japanese young-leaf compound.
Wakachi, wakatsu, wakatta means dividing or distinguishing. The principal parts identify the verb before its examples.

Iefiuo vacatçu means distinguishing right and wrong, as confirmed by the Portuguese good-and-evil gloss. The weak initial type is read as consonantal I rather than the OCR t; this preserves the historical spelling while leaving the initial identification a minor caveat.

runs.text: mal. ¶ Item, Repartir, ou fazer differẽ-

lines.note: Completes the contrast with evil, then adds dividing, distributing, or making a distinction. Differẽ- continues into ça on the next physical row.
Introduces the example that dying makes no distinction of rank, high or low, rich or poor. Qixen, jǒgue, and divided fin- begin the social contrasts.
Completes finpucu, poverty and wealth, in the negative vacatazu: death does not distinguish between them. The Portuguese begins the same assertion, with dif- continued below.

runs.text: ferença de altos & baixos, nem de ricos &

lines.note: Completes differença and contrasts high and low, rich and poor. The printed Portuguese paraphrases the Japanese social oppositions rather than translating each compound separately.
Pobres completes the rich-and-poor pair. This short final row closes the death example.
Wakakusa here means new grass or herbs, directly matched by eruas nouas in the gloss.

runs.text: Certa conſeição de cheiro, ou per-

lines.note: A second wakakusa entry names a scented preparation or incense. The scan and OCR conſeição are retained: the tall type lacks a secure f cross-stroke, although the contextual Portuguese word would be confeição. This allograph remains a nonblocking uncertainty.
Completes perfume and specifies that the fragrant preparation is burned. This distinguishes the scented-product entry from ordinary young grass.
Wakadachi denotes new shoots or tender small branches. The Portuguese vergonteas and raminhos describe the growth itself.
Tenros completes raminhos tenros, tender small branches. The worn r was conflated with neighboring strokes in OCR temos.
Wakago is the young son of a nobleman. The dictionary gives a social restriction beyond the general sense of a young child.
Wakagimi is a prince still a child, or the son of a great lord. Minino retains the printed historical vowel.
Completes the alternative definition as a great lord's son; this continuation belongs to wakagimi.

runs.text: Couſa noua, & tenra, ou de pouca ida-

lines.note: Wakai describes something new, tender, young in age, or newly born. The scan reads pouca, correcting OCR poura, and ida- continues as idade.
Completes idade and adds newly born; Vacai fito begins the example of a young person. The final word is fito, not the OCR fita.

runs.text: Homem mancebo como de 15. annos tè 25.

lines.note: Defines the example as a young man of roughly fifteen to twenty-five years. The numbers are part of the historical dictionary's description.
Pouco mais, ou menos qualifies the age range as approximate. It is a continuation of the young-man example.
Wakasa is the nominal derivative meaning youth or youngness, listed beneath the adjective wakai.
Wakoo is the contracted adverbial form associated with wakai. Only Vacǒ. is printed; the OCR addition Ait. Iamoa has no corresponding text on this row.

runs.text: Certos limos do mar de folha larga

lines.note: Wakame is described as a broad-leaved seaweed. The dictionary's botanical description, rather than a modern taxonomic name, is retained.
Nouos and tenros describe the seaweed as new and tender, completing the wakame definition.
Wakamidori is glossed as new small branches, emphasizing fresh growth.

runs.text: Agoa noua. i, que ſe toma no

lines.note: Wakamizu is new water, with the following explanation specifying the ceremonial first drawing of the year.
The water is taken on the first day of the new year. Vacamiz- begins the example across the physical line break.
Wakamizu wo kumu or mukayuru means drawing or welcoming that new water; Latin l introduces the alternative verb. Tomar desta begins the Portuguese rendering.
Agoa noua completes the explanation of drawing the first new water of the year.
Wakamono is a young man, directly glossed mancebo.
Wakamonodate means acting or wishing to appear young. The headword starts at the ordinary entry margin, so the OCR indentation is removed.
Completes mostrar and specifies an old person trying to appear young. Vacamo- starts the repeated noun in the example.
Nodateuo ſuru completes wakamonodate wo suru, doing what the preceding definition describes. Idem refers to that same meaning.
Wakamusha means a young soldier or warrior, matching soldado mancebo.

runs.text: Verſo de Iapão, & verſo da China q̃

lines.note: Wakan combines Japanese verse and Chinese verse; the latter is named on the following line. This is an ordinary unindented headword row, and China retains its visible capital.
The Chinese verse is called Xi, shi. The Japanese term is embedded in the Portuguese naming clause and is printed upright.

runs.text: Folhasde nabos que ſe colhe, ou comẽ

lines.note: Wakana denotes turnip leaves gathered or eaten on the seventh day of the New Year period; the timing continues at the top of column 2. The tightly set Folhasde is retained. A faint mark above the final e of colhe is not securely a tilde, so the unmarked OCR form is retained.

Completes the wakana definition: the leaves are gathered or eaten on the seventh day of the first month, named Xǒguachi within Portuguese. The scan shows a caron, not the OCR tilde, over o; Vacanauo starts the example.

runs.text: Colher estas folhas nouas neste dia.

lines.note: Tsumu completes wakana wo tsumu, gathering these fresh leaves on that day. The Portuguese restates the action and occasion.
Wakane means tender roots of the aquatic plant glossed golfão. Fa- starts hasu no wakane across the line boundary; no modern botanical species is imposed.
Completes Faſuno vacane, tender lotus roots. Idem repeats the definition, then a comparison begins between the newest growth and ordinary thicker growth.
The newest and tenderest roots are called Fai; the Portuguese next turns to the ordinary ones. Fai is an upright Japanese name embedded in the explanation.

The ordinary, already thick roots are called Faſu. The damaged word is read groſsas, with one long and one short s, correcting OCR grojas; the weak types leave a minor allograph caveat. Faſu is the Japanese term within the Portuguese naming clause.
Wakaki is a young tree, directly glossed aruore noua.
Wakare, wakaruru, wakareta means separating or parting. The historical ruru principal part is preserved.
The example describes parting from parents, spouse, children, and similar family members. The initial Voya represents oya, with the source's positional v spelling.
The Portuguese renders the family separation as parting from parents, wives, children, and so forth. Its plural wording is retained.
Wakare is the noun separation or parting. Apartamento here has that historical sense, not a modern dwelling.
Wakari is glossed as dividing or separating. The abbreviated principal part u is visibly printed and is retained, although ru would be the regular continuation of the verb.
Touzai ni wakaru means separating toward east and west. Diuidirſe corrects OCR Diaidirſe and introduces the directional gloss.

runs.text: pera a parte do Oriẽte, & Poente. ¶

lines.note: Completes the east-and-west translation, then begins a Christian Japanese example with Ecleſiano, of the Church. The OCR split between italic E and deſuno misread the upright borrowed church name plus no.
Sacramentos ua nanatçuni vacaru says that the Church's sacraments divide into seven. Sacramentos is upright within the Japanese example; Os Sa- begins the Portuguese translation.

runs.text: cramentos da Igreja ſe diuidem em ſete. ¶

lines.note: Completes Sacramentos and says that the Church's sacraments are divided into seven. The scan reads ſete, not OCR fete; Ri- starts the next Japanese example.
Ri ga wakaru or wakaranu contrasts understanding with not understanding a reason or explanation. The final vowel of the positive form is u rather than OCR a.

runs.text: tenderſe bem algũa couſa, ou não ſe entender,

lines.note: Completes entenderſe and explains whether a matter is understood well or is not understood. The final entender retains its visible r, omitted by OCR.
Adds that the reasoning or explanation may fail to become clear. Arrezoamento is the printed historical form.
Wakarime is the place or boundary at which one thing separates from another. The compressed final hũa modifies couſa on the next row.

runs.text: couſa ſe aparta, ou diuide de outra.

lines.note: Completes the boundary definition: a thing parts or divides from another. The phrase ou diuide is restored from the tightly set words.
Wakasaburai refers to young men of the warrior or noble class, matching mancebos fidalgos.

runs.text: Mancebos, q̃ ſeruem a algum ſenhor.

lines.note: Wakatou names young attendants serving a lord. The damaged t in Vacatǒ is supported by its surviving stroke and the repeated Matavacatǒ below; the later-consulted NINJAL index confirms the lexical identification.

runs.text: ¶ Item, No Ximo, Moço de ſeruiço.

lines.note: Adds the Ximo regional sense of a serving boy. Ximo is a Japanese place or regional label within the Portuguese usage explanation.
Matawakatou refers to young soldiers or retainers at a further subordinate level. The Portuguese relative clause continues below.

runs.text: ſeruem a criados honrados dalgum ſenhor.

lines.note: These youths serve a lord's honored retainers. The scan reads ſenhor, with long s, not OCR lenhor.
Wakashi, wakasu, wakaita means heating water, wine, and similar liquids. The historical aita principal part is retained rather than modernized.
Gives yu wo wakasu and explicitly rejects the following mizu wo wakasu form. The divided Miz- is entirely upright Japanese text; the OCR italic i and missing z are corrected.
Zuuo vacaſu completes mizu wo wakasu, the expression rejected by the preceding usage note. The doubled z spans the physical break Miz- / zuuo. This is a historical judgment in the dictionary.
Wakashu first means young men; the second sense concerns a boy with whom someone has an illicit sexual relationship. Moço de is completed by the relative clause below.

runs.text: que alguem vſa mal acrecentando lhe algua pa-

lines.note: Continues the euphemistic definition and explains that the sense is specified by adding another word. The compressed end is read algua pa-, without supplying an uncertain tilde; pa- continues into laura on the next row.

Completes palaura and gives sono hito no wakashu, that person's youth or partner. The compressed Portuguese ending is O cõ-, continuing as cõplice below; the separate article O was conflated with the following word by OCR.
Plice completes cõplice, and deße homem identifies the partner of that man. The wording belongs to the historical gloss's euphemistic sexual sense.
Wakayagi, wakayagu, wakayaida means trees budding or putting out new growth. Aruores, not OCR aruoris, is supported by the compressed ending; the final punctuation has a comma tail.

runs.text: ¶ Item, per met. Remoçar como quando hũ

lines.note: Introduces the figurative sense of becoming young again, illustrated by an old person dressing anew. The final hũ is compressed near the gutter but supplies the article for velho.
Completes that illustration, then begins Fitono qi, a person's spirit. The scan supports upright Fitono rather than the OCR mixed-font Fitomo.
Qi, alternatively kokoro, is the spirit or heart that becomes youthful. The Portuguese begins mostrar animo; ani is visible at the right edge without a secure terminal hyphen.
Completes animo and adds youthful vigor. Mizzuga va- begins the separate example of water being new at the new year.

runs.text: Ser agoa noua. i, do anno nouo.

lines.note: Cayagu completes wakayagu, and the translation identifies new water as water of the new year. The final word reads nouo, correcting OCR nour.
Wakayeda means a new or tender branch; the historical ye sequence is retained.

runs.text: Hum modo de pintura de circulos

lines.note: Wachigaye denotes a painted pattern of interlaced circles. The compressed ending reads circulos, without the OCR's invented terminal hyphen.

runs.text: entretecidos que ha nas coſtas dos Beǒbus, ou

lines.note: The circles occur on the backs of folding screens, here called Beǒbus. The caron is visible over o; the plural term is embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
The pattern also appears on boys' clothing. This completes the decorative-pattern definition rather than introducing another item.
Wachou is glossed as Japan. The circumflex in Vachô is retained as printed.

runs.text: Filho de fidalgo, ou peßoa honrada.

lines.note: Wakou names the son of a nobleman or an honorable person. Its caron distinguishes the printed long vowel from the preceding circumflex entry.
Wakoku is equated with Nippon and glossed Japan. Nippon is a Japanese synonym after i, so it is not an embedded-Portuguese typeface term.

runs.text: Inſtrumento como ſarilho em que debão

lines.note: Waku is an implement resembling a reel for winding spun thread. The compressed final verb is read debão, preserving the apparent printed e rather than normalizing it to expected dobão; that weak vowel remains a nonblocking caveat; the object is anticipated in the separate bottom catchword.

The isolated italic o fiado, is the bottom-right catchword for the continuing reel definition. Its position and smaller type distinguish it from the body row; the following page is not supplied in this package.
